figures.label: Figure 1
figures.caption: The illustration of two practical challenges: class imbalance and test agnostics. Existing method is only focused on uniform tests in federated settings.
figures.headline: Existing federated methods focus only on uniform tests, leaving class imbalance and unknown test distributions as separate challenges.
citing_sentences: As illustrated in Fig. 1, this assumption rarely holds in practice as the test distribution is often unknown.

figures.label: Figure 2
figures.caption: CReFF performance degradation with reduced training data size across different test distributions. Performance drops significantly as training data decreases from 100% to 10%, with Backward50 test showing the most severe degradation
figures.headline: CReFF accuracy drops as training data shrinks from 100% to 10%, most severely on the Backward50 test.
citing_sentences: The train-test distribution discrepancy becomes more pronounced when data is limited, as demonstrated in Fig. 2.

figures.label: Figure 3
figures.caption: Expert classifier specialization demonstrates that each classifier achieves optimal performance on its corresponding test distribution while maintaining competitive accuracy across other test distribution.
figures.headline: Each expert classifier reaches its best accuracy on the test distribution it was retrained for, and stays competitive elsewhere.
citing_sentences: Our experimental analysis on CIFAR10-LT, illustrated in Figure 3, reveals that retraining classifiers on federated features with different distribution yields varying performance in different tests.

figures.label: Figure 4
figures.caption: GTAFL framework workflow: (1) Clients receive global model and expert parameters, then perform local training with GI-GDS sampling and gradient computation. (2) Clients transmit class-wise gradients and model parameters to the server. (3) Server performs aggregation, expert retraining using optimized global federated features, and self-supervised refinement with unlabeled data. (4) The server sends the updated global model and expert classifiers parameters to clients. (5) Expert ensemble inference for test-agnostic prediction.
figures.headline: The workflow runs five steps per round, from client sampling and gradient computation to expert ensemble inference.
citing_sentences: As illustrated in Fig. 4, the proposed GTAFL framework consists of four components: data sampling, expert classifiers retraining, self-supervised refinement, and class-wise experts ensemble.

figures.label: Figure 5
figures.caption: Performance comparison of GTAFL and CReFF on varying CIFAR10 data fractions. GTAFL demonstrates greater robustness as the data size decreases. (FW50 = Forward50, Uni. = Uniform, BW50 = Backward50). When the data fraction reduces to 10% of original dataset, GTAFL outperforms CReFF by nearly 5%. For more details, please refer to VI-C2.
figures.headline: GTAFL stays ahead of CReFF as training data shrinks, outperforming it by nearly 5% at 10% of the data.
citing_sentences: Figure 5 presents the comparative analysis between GTAFL and CReFF across different data availability conditions.

figures.label: Figure 6
figures.caption: Sensitivity analysis of GFF Imbalance on CIFAR10-LT. A larger $\lambda$ induces a more skewed GFF distribution across expert classifiers.
figures.headline: Larger lambda values make the synthetic feature distribution more skewed across expert classifiers, shown on CIFAR10-LT.
citing_sentences: Figure 6 reports the sensitivity of $\lambda$, and it controls the distributional imbalance of the synthetic global federated features (GFF) used for expert classifier retraining.

abstract: In healthcare, protecting patient privacy is crucial due to the sensitivity of medical data and its extensive accessibility. Federated Learning (FL) offers a decentralized and privacy-preserving training paradigm, making it an ideal solution for healthcare applications. A critical challenge in healthcare is that real-world medical data often exhibits long-tailed distributions in local and global views. Existing methods addressing long-tailed FL problem typically assume that the model will be evaluated on uniform test data distribution. However, Practical test data in healthcare systems is often agnostic and unpredictable, leading to potential model failures in real-world scenarios. In this paper, we introduce a novel task termed Test-Agnostic Long-Tailed Federated Learning and propose GTAFL, a comprehensive framework to address this challenge. During the training stage, GTAFL employs adaptive re-sampling, expert classifier retraining, and self-supervised learning to correct biased classifiers and distorted feature spaces caused by long-tailed training distributions. During the inference stage, an ensemble mechanism combines retrained expert classifiers to handle test data with unknown distributions. Extensive experiments on CIFAR10 and two medical datasets manifest that our framework outperforms other state-of-the art methods. The code is available at https://github.com/cgy-lavine/GTAFL

sections.body:
Federated learning (FL) lets clients train a shared model without sharing raw data, which suits Internet of Medical Things settings. The paper says class imbalance is common in medical data, and that existing long-tailed FL methods assume uniform test distributions, an assumption it says rarely holds (Fig. 1).

It names two challenges: class imbalance at both global and local levels, and generalization to unknown test distributions. Training several expert models on clients is impractical on edge devices, so GTAFL retrains expert classifiers on the server using global federated features. It also applies self-supervised learning to an unlabeled test set.

The contributions are the new task, the GTAFL framework with four components, and an analysis of synthetic global federated features.
sections.heading: Introduction
sections.headline: Federated learning on long-tailed medical data assumes uniform test sets, so GTAFL targets unknown test distributions.

sections.body:
The section defines FL with K clients, local datasets, and FedAvg weighted averaging over selected clients in each round. Class counts are kept per client and globally. The imbalance factor IF is the maximum global class count divided by the minimum.

The training set follows a long-tailed distribution with imbalance factor IF. The test set has an unknown class distribution that may be forward, uniform, or backward relative to the training long tail. The objective is to minimize expected cross-entropy loss over that unknown test distribution.

Table I lists the notation, including forward, uniform, and backward experts. This section reports no experiments.
sections.heading: Preliminaries and Problem Formulation
sections.headline: Formal setup defines federated learning, the imbalance factor, and the objective over forward, uniform, and backward test distributions.

sections.body:
The motivation study uses CIFAR10-LT. Retraining classifiers on federated features with different distributions gives each classifier its best accuracy on the matching test distribution, shown in Figure 3. Figure 2 shows CReFF accuracy falling as training data drops from 100% to 10%, most severely on Backward50.

The overview lists five steps per round: sampling on clients, client uploads, server aggregation with expert retraining and self-supervised refinement, redistribution, and expert voting at inference. Expert classifiers are retrained on optimized global federated features. The feature extractor is then refined on unlabeled medical images, and the text says no patient metadata is used.
sections.heading: Motivation and Overview
sections.headline: Each distribution-specific classifier performs best on its own test distribution, which motivates retraining one expert per distribution.

sections.body:
Sampling weights for each client and class interpolate between inverse local frequency and inverse global frequency. The mixing parameter is 1 when the cosine similarity between local and global class-count vectors is below tau = 0.9, and 0 otherwise.

Expert classifiers for forward, uniform, and backward priors share one feature extractor. The server optimizes global federated features by minimizing cosine distance between their induced gradients and aggregated client gradients. It then retrains each expert while freezing the feature extractor.

Refinement applies a contrastive loss (NT-Xent) to unlabeled images. At inference, one expert per distribution type casts an equally weighted hard vote. This section reports no experiments.
sections.heading: Methodology
sections.headline: Method has four components: sampling weights interpolating local and global signals, expert classifier retraining on synthetic features, self-supervised refinement, and weighted voting.

sections.body:
CIFAR10-LT has 50,000 training and 10,000 test images across 10 classes. PathMNIST-LT has 89,996 training and 7,180 test samples across 9 classes. OCTMNIST-LT has 97,477 training and 1,000 test samples across 4 classes. All three use an imbalance factor of 50, and clients are split with a Dirichlet distribution at alpha 0.5.

Federated training uses 20 clients, 40% participation per round, and ResNet-8. It runs 200 rounds on CIFAR10-LT and PathMNIST-LT and 100 rounds on OCTMNIST-LT. SGD uses learning rate 0.1.

Six baselines are compared: FedAvg, FedProx, BalanceFL, CReFF, FedGraB, and FedLoGe.
sections.heading: Experiments Setup
sections.headline: Experiments use three datasets with imbalance factor 50, 20 clients, and six baseline federated methods.

sections.body:
Table III reports accuracy across 11 test distributions. On CIFAR10-LT, GTAFL averages 75.02% against 73.69% for CReFF, and reaches 78.14% at Backward50. On PathMNIST-LT it averages 77.71%, with 83.87% at Forward50. On OCTMNIST-LT it averages 66.42%. FedAvg and FedProx score higher at Forward50, which the paper attributes to assigning test samples to majority classes.

Tables VI and VII report CIFAR10-LT overhead: client time 1712s against 1376s for CReFF, server time 4687s, and 316 MB of extra communication versus FedAvg over 200 rounds. Table VIII shows hard, soft, and confidence-weighted voting differ by less than 0.006.

The ablation table is cut from the supplied text.
sections.heading: Experiments
sections.headline: GTAFL reaches 75.02% average accuracy on CIFAR10-LT, above CReFF's 73.69%, and the best average on both medical datasets.

sections.body:
The related work covers long-tailed federated learning and test-agnostic learning. Federated methods named include re-sampling, classifier retraining such as CReFF, prototype-based RUCR, and contrastive Moon. Centralized test-agnostic methods named include LADE, which uses prior knowledge of test distributions for post-adjustment, and SADE, which trains experts with specialized losses.

The section argues that clients often lack resources to train several models, and that missing classes at clients degrade experts. GTAFL instead retrains experts on the server and ensembles them at inference. The authors state they are the first to identify and formulate test-agnostic long-tailed federated learning.
sections.heading: Related Work
sections.headline: Related work groups long-tailed and test-agnostic methods, and the authors claim to be first to formulate this federated task.

sections.body:
The discussion covers privacy. Gradient and model inversion attacks may partially reconstruct training data, which the section calls especially concerning for healthcare. The authors say GTAFL is compatible with client-side differential privacy applied to expert gradients and model updates, through per-example clipping and calibrated noise. They do not report privacy experiments.

The section names one limitation: relatively modest accuracy on majority classes under backward distributions, described as a trade-off.

Future work lists adaptive noise schedules with secure aggregation, more efficient contrastive objectives, handling of excessively large lambda values that reverse expert specialization, and evaluation on broader medical datasets.
sections.heading: Discussion
sections.headline: Privacy risks from gradient inversion are discussed, with differential privacy proposed as compatible but unevaluated, and majority-class accuracy noted as a limitation.

sections.body:
The conclusion restates the task and the GTAFL approach of ensembling expert classifiers. Global federated features are used for privacy-preserving expert retraining. The conclusion claims performance across distribution shifts without serious degradation on reverse or imbalanced distributions.

It states that experiments show GTAFL outperforms other long-tailed federated learning methods and frames the framework as relevant to healthcare, where privacy and tolerance of distribution shift are both critical.

The conclusion adds no new numbers. The evidence for these claims is the comparison on three datasets reported in the experiments section.
sections.heading: Conclusion
sections.headline: The paper concludes that GTAFL outperforms long-tailed federated baselines across three datasets and distribution shifts.
